statement: Sequoyah (George Guess/Gist), a monolingual Cherokee speaker who never learned to read or write English, began developing a writing system c. 1809 after observing literate soldiers during the War of 1812/Creek War (including the Battle of Horseshoe Bend). He first attempted an unmanageable logographic (one-symbol-per-word) system, then pivoted to analyzing spoken Cherokee's syllable inventory, completing an 86-character (later 85) syllabary by 1821; his daughter Ayokeh (Ahyokah) demonstrated the system worked for someone who had not helped design it. Formally adopted by the Cherokee National Council in 1825; the bilingual Cherokee Phoenix newspaper launched 1828. His character shapes resemble Latin/Greek/Cyrillic letterforms he had seen but could not read, while sound values are unrelated to those alphabets' actual values — since he had no access to the source letters' phonetic values, only their shapes, this is a clean STIMULUS_DIFFUSION case: concept and some visual stock borrowed, sign-to-sound mapping invented from scratch.

notes: The often-repeated ~90% post-syllabary Cherokee literacy figure traces to Ellen Cushman and Theda Perdue ("The Sequoyah Syllabary and Cultural Revitalization," 1994) but could not be independently traced to a period census or contemporaneous quantitative source this session — treat as a widely cited scholarly estimate, not a hard count.
